item.title: "Don't fear the REAPer" or how DS chose a local LLM
item.description:
Over the past few months, I've tested a bunch of local LLMs that my hardware can handle and came to a conclusion that's already obvious to many: for coding tasks, there are no real alternatives to Qwen models. So, I decided to delete all unnecessary models from my disk to keep only the "workhorses." At that moment, a video with a tier-list caught my eye, where I recognized many familiar models. And then it all started...

item.title: Fresh scientific papers on AI, agents, and everything else. September 2026: multimodal AI and robotics
item.description:
Hello, Habr! In the previous part of the digest, I collected scientific papers on LLMs, agent development, and security, and now I'll move on to images, speech, and robots. In total, this digest contains 17 studies on CV, speech, robots, and other systems that combine different types of data. In some studies, scientists tested real manipulators and drones; in others, they limited themselves to simulation. In each review, we clarify how the tests were conducted, as good test results are not a guarantee that a robot will cope with the task just as well in real conditions. For the most illustrative papers, we have added illustrations from the original publications. Read more

Original Russian article on Habr

item.title: Software Robot vs. "Smart" Software Robot vs. Intelligent Agent: A First Look
item.description:
There are so many robots now! They come in different types and for different purposes, aimed at mechanical and "intellectual" work. How to distinguish one type from another, or are they just marketing labels for the same thing? Valery Pozdnyakov, lead specialist at the R&D Department of JSC "Greenatom", analyzes regulatory documents – from orders of the Ministry of Digital Development and the Ministry of Industry and Trade to GOST standards – and identifies the characteristics that distinguish a software robot from a "smart" one, and finally, from an intelligent agent. Spoiler: the line exists, but it's thinner than it seems. Read more

item.title: How We Scaled Medical Image Processing with Ray. Part 1
item.description:
Hello everyone, this is the ML team from "Third Opinion Platform" company. We specialize in artificial intelligence in medicine. A significant portion of our company's products are built around computer vision tasks in the field of radiation diagnostics. The data we work with includes X-rays, fluorographies, CT scans of various body parts, and mammographies. Medical organizations send us studies and receive processed results with various findings: localized pathological areas, measurements, probability assessments of pathology, and other data. We'll discuss the specifics of this work in more detail another time. Today, we'll talk about Ray and why it became necessary in our architecture. Read more

item.title: One phrase from the team lead in the prompt cut task estimates by a fifth
item.description:
Estimating story points using neural networks seems like a quick way to speed up sprint planning. But just one phrase about how much the team lead thinks a task should cost is enough to change the estimates of two LLMs by about 20%. In an experiment with historical Jira tasks, we look at how the anchoring effect works in poker planning and why a sum close to the team's estimate doesn't necessarily mean an accurate assessment. Find out the results

item.title: How to Integrate AI Agents into Development: Requirements, Architecture, and Quality Control
item.description:
How to integrate AI agents into team development and control the quality of changes? The introduction of AI into development often starts with a simple requirement: use agents and release features faster. And even among developers, there's a notion that they are now "meat proxies." But questions quickly arise: who checks how the agent understood the task, what decisions can be entrusted to it, and how to ensure that the new feature hasn't broken existing ones? Read more

item.title: How a website can get into Claude's search results: search and user bots are important, not ClaudeBot
item.description:
Anthropic has three bots with different tasks: one collects texts for training AI models, another indexes pages for Claude's web search, and a third visits when a user asks to read a page. Each can be blocked separately in robots.txt, but sites often block the ones they depend on. Crawl Readiness checked the top 1000 sites in October 2026: Claude-SearchBot is blocked by 63 out of 569 sites with a robots.txt, meaning one in nine. A page only becomes a source for Claude if it's seen by the search engine it uses and if the search and user bots are allowed on the site. The training ClaudeBot has little impact on this, so if the goal was just to prevent text from being used for training, blocking only that bot would suffice. Read more

item.title: Drag me into harness. Part 4. Fat harness: intent is everything
item.description:
Fat harness is a software loop surrounding the model that takes on most of the verifiable decisions: request normalization, routing, context requirements, policy, permissions, workflow execution, long-term state, and verification. The model remains useful at the boundary where understanding human text is required, but does not become the sole source of truth. This is an architecture in which a significant portion of decisions are moved from the probabilistic model to explicit contracts and ordinary code. Read more

item.title: The Dubiousness of AI Alignment
item.description:
As AI technology rapidly advances, warnings about its safety are becoming more frequent and louder. The most common proposed solution is a procedure called alignment, which aims to align AI interests with human interests. Otherwise, AI might develop its own interests that diverge from human interests, potentially leading it to eliminate humans as an obstacle. This approach assumes there's nothing objective about humanity's interests, allowing advanced AI to develop different interests. However, this view has a conceptual flaw: the antagonism isn't between human and AI interests, but between the interests of different human groups. In this context, AI alignment itself poses a genuine global threat. How can advanced AI interests be closer to humanity's global interests than the interests of specific human groups? This article explores this question.

item.title: Sliced the image into fragments: what helped small defects and what broke large ones
item.description:
Hello, Habr! My name is Maxim, I am a student at MIREA. This is a continuation of the article "Small defects are lost, and the metric is silent". In it, I compared Mask R-CNN and YOLO on 1812 production images with car damage and ended up with tiling: if the image is cut into pieces, small objects will not be compressed along with the entire frame. I eventually got to tiling, and it wasn't a straight path. Almost every attempt fixed something and broke something at the same time. Below is a story about the steps I took, where I made mistakes, and what conclusions I drew from it. Read more
